title: The Handshake in a Post-Handshake World
hook: The pandemic broke the handshake's monopoly, and now many meetings begin with a small negotiation over whether to touch at all.
why:
For most of the last century, the handshake was the default greeting of working life in much of the world. You shook hands at an interview, at the start of a meeting, on closing a deal and at a funeral. Men were taught to do it firmly, look the other man in the eye and never offer a limp hand. Few greetings carried more weight or more advice.

Then, in 2020, it stopped almost overnight. When it returned, it returned as an option rather than a rule. Some people now reach for a hand without thinking, others hold back, and many hesitate for half a second to see what the other person will do. The chapter on male greetings in Part III dealt with how men read and match each other's offers. This chapter looks at the handshake at work: what the research says it does, what a good one involves, why interviews care about it, what the germ evidence shows, how the pandemic changed it, and how to offer, accept or decline one gracefully when you cannot be sure what the other person wants.

teach.p:
It is easy to dismiss the handshake as an empty ritual, but there is evidence that it shapes how an encounter is judged. In a 2012 study, Sanda Dolcos, Florin Dolcos and their colleagues showed people short animated scenes of a host greeting a visitor in an office. In half of the scenes the two shook hands before talking; in the rest they did not. The people watching rated the encounters that began with a handshake more positively, and a handshake softened the bad impression left when one of the figures behaved in a cold or avoidant way.

The researchers also scanned the brains of the people watching. A region involved in processing reward was more active when the scene began with a handshake. That does not mean a handshake is a drug. It does suggest that people treat a handshake as a signal of good intent, and that the signal colours how everything after it is read.

There are limits to what this shows. These were observers watching cartoons, not people shaking hands themselves, and the study did not test whether a handshake changes the outcome of a real meeting. But it fits with ordinary experience: an encounter that opens with a warm, mutual greeting feels like it has started on the right foot, and one that opens with an awkward refusal or a missed hand feels slightly off, however friendly the conversation that follows.

The figures here shake hands in profile, at arm's length, meeting midway. Neither has reached across the other's space. The greeting took two seconds, and it has already told each of them something about the other.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if encounters that began with a handshake were judged no differently from those that did not. In this study they were judged more positively, though the participants were observers rather than the people shaking hands.

teach.p:
The most familiar advice about handshakes is to make them firm. In 2000 William Chaplin and his colleagues put that advice to a test. Four trained coders, two men and two women, each shook hands twice with 112 people and rated the handshakes on several features: the strength of the grip, its vigour, its duration, how completely the hands met, and whether the person made eye contact. The people being greeted also completed personality questionnaires.

The handshakes turned out to be consistent: the same person tended to shake hands in the same way on different occasions and with different coders. A firm handshake, in the full sense of a complete grip, some vigour, a reasonable duration and eye contact, went with more favourable first impressions. It also went with being more extraverted and expressive, and less shy and anxious.

Men's handshakes were firmer on average, but women with firm handshakes made favourable impressions too, and the authors noted that they did not seem to pay the price women often pay for behaving assertively. A later study by Frank Bernieri and Kristen Petty suggested that shaking hands may help men judge one trait more accurately: how conscientious the other person is.

Notice what firm does not mean. It does not mean crushing. The coders were rating a complete, confident grip, not raw pressure. The figure here offers an open, ready posture. A good handshake is an extension of that: the whole hand, a grip that matches the other person's, two or three seconds, and a look at their face.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if handshake quality were unrelated to first impressions. In Chaplin's study, a complete, confident grip with eye contact went with more favourable impressions, though the links to personality were modest and later work has qualified them.
teach.pullQuote: Firm means complete, not crushing: the whole hand, a matched grip, a few seconds and a look at the other person's face.

teach.p:
Job interviews are where handshake advice is most anxious and most insistent. In 2008 Greg Stewart and his colleagues ran mock interviews with 98 students. Trained raters scored each student's handshake, and interviewers made recommendations about whether to hire. Students with better handshakes received more favourable hiring recommendations, even after the researchers accounted for physical appearance and dress.

The study also suggested why. More extraverted students tended to give better handshakes, and the handshake appeared to carry part of the link between extraversion and the interviewers' judgments. Women's handshakes were rated lower on average, but women were not rated as less suitable, and the link between handshake and rating may have been stronger for them.

It would be easy to draw the wrong lesson. The study does not show that training your grip will get you a job. A handshake is a small, visible sample of social ease, and the people with good handshakes were probably at ease in other ways too: in how they sat, spoke and looked at the interviewer. The handshake may have been one sign of that ease rather than its cause.

The useful lesson is narrower. Interviewers notice the opening seconds, and a handshake that is limp, sweaty or crushing can start things badly. Practise a few times with a friend until a complete, matched grip feels natural, then stop thinking about it. A later chapter on interviews looks at what interviewers can and cannot read, from both sides of the desk. The figure here waits upright before being called in, hands loose rather than wringing.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if handshake quality bore no relation to interview ratings. In Stewart's study it did, even with appearance and dress accounted for, though the handshake may be a sign of social ease rather than a cause of success.

teach.p:
Most bad handshakes fall into a few familiar kinds. The crusher squeezes hard enough to hurt, often as a show of strength, and leaves the other person with the impression of someone who competes where he should connect. The fish is a limp, passive hand that gives nothing back. The fingertip grip catches only the other person's fingers, usually because someone reached too early. The pump goes on shaking for too long. The yank pulls the other person off balance towards you.

There are also handshakes that try to say something about status. Popular books describe turning your hand palm down on top of the other person's as a dominance move, or adding a second hand on their wrist or shoulder to show warmth or control. These ideas are widely repeated but little tested. What is clear is that any handshake that makes the other person feel managed tends to be read as a power play, however it was meant.

For many people the real problem is simpler: anxiety. Hands get cold and damp when you are nervous, and a damp handshake is one of the things people dread most. The practical fixes are unglamorous. Hold any cold drink in your left hand, so your right hand stays dry and warm. Wipe your palm discreetly on a handkerchief or your trousers before you stand. Keep your hands loose and still, not wringing, in the minutes beforehand.

The figure here wrings his hands while waiting, a sign of nerves that also tends to make palms damper. Letting them rest open, or holding something, gives the anxiety less to work with.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if crushing, limp or prolonged handshakes were judged as favourably as complete, matched ones. Chaplin's coders rated the features of a good handshake together, and grips at either extreme rarely make a good impression.
teach.pullQuote: Any handshake that makes the other person feel managed is read as a power play, whatever you meant by it.

teach.p:
Doctors and infection specialists had worried about handshakes long before 2020. Hands carry bacteria and viruses, and a handshake brings two palms into firm, prolonged contact. In 2014 Sara Mela and David Whitworth at Aberystwyth University compared greetings directly. They had people wear sterile gloves, dipped one gloved hand in a harmless strain of bacteria, and measured how much transferred during a handshake, a high five and a fist bump.

The handshake transferred the most. A high five transferred considerably less, and a fist bump far less again. Longer and stronger handshakes transferred more, which makes sense: more contact, for longer, over a larger area. The authors suggested the fist bump as a more hygienic alternative, particularly in hospitals, where staff greet large numbers of people and infection matters most.

The study has limits. It used gloves rather than bare hands, and a single kind of bacteria, so it gives a sense of the relative difference rather than the risk of any particular greeting. Hand washing matters more than any choice of greeting, and Whitworth himself doubted that a no-contact greeting would ever replace the handshake entirely.

But the principle is useful. When you are ill, when the other person is frail or unwell, or when you are in a hospital or care home, the kindest greeting may be the one with the least contact. The figures here bump fists: brief, light and involving only the knuckles. It is informal, and not right for every setting, but it carries some of the warmth of touch at a fraction of the contact.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if a fist bump transferred as many bacteria as a handshake. In Mela and Whitworth's study it transferred far fewer, though the experiment used gloves rather than bare hands.

teach.p:
In April 2020, early in the pandemic, Anthony Fauci, then the leading infectious disease official in the United States, said on a podcast that he did not think people should ever shake hands again. For a while, in many countries, almost nobody did. People improvised: elbow bumps, foot taps, nods, waves, and the hand placed on the heart that many cultures already used.

The handshake did not disappear. In much of the world it returned, but not entirely and not for everyone. Some people dropped it for good, especially those who are older, unwell, caring for someone vulnerable, or simply relieved to have a reason not to touch strangers. Others never stopped. The result is that the handshake is no longer the single expected greeting at work. It is one option among several, and the choice is now often made on the spot, by both people, in the second before they meet.

That second is where things can go wrong. One person's hand comes out while the other's stays down, or two people hesitate at once and neither moves. The awkwardness is small but real, and it falls hardest on the person who offered and was not met.

A useful default is to signal before you touch. As you approach, let your hand begin to come forward, slowly enough that the other person can respond, and watch what they do. If their hand comes out, shake it. If it stays down, turn the movement into a hand on your heart or a small open gesture and nod. Here a man offers his hand and a woman answers with a hand on her heart, a greeting that says she is glad to meet him without the touch.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if almost everyone had returned to shaking hands as automatically as before 2020. Many people did, but many did not, which is why reading the offer has become part of the greeting.

teach.p:
Because the handshake is now a choice, it helps to know how to make that choice well. When you are unsure, let the other person lead. A host, an older person or someone more senior often sets the greeting, and matching their choice is rarely wrong. If you offer a hand and it is not taken, withdraw it without fuss, smile and say something warm. The person who declined was probably not rejecting you.

Some people do not shake hands for reasons of faith. Many observant Muslims and Orthodox Jews do not shake hands with someone of the opposite sex outside their close family, and may offer a hand on the heart or a nod instead. In parts of Asia a bow, a wai or palms pressed together may be the expected greeting. Others decline because of health, disability, pain in their hands or a history that makes touch from strangers unwelcome. You do not need to know the reason. You only need to accept the choice gracefully.

If you are the one declining, do it warmly and early, before the other person's hand is fully out. Smile, nod, place a hand on your heart or raise it in a small wave, and say something like, I'm not shaking hands at the moment, but it's very good to meet you. The warmth of the words and face does the work the handshake would have done. Most people will take their cue from you and move on in a second.

The figure here greets with palms pressed together, the wai used in Thailand. Greetings like this are complete in themselves. They are not lesser versions of a handshake, and offering one is not a refusal to connect.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if declining a handshake warmly were usually taken as an insult. In practice a clear, friendly alternative offered early is accepted by most people, and the awkward moments come from hesitation rather than refusal.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Stepping in too far for the grip
poseGallery.annotation: A handshake works at arm's length. Closing the gap as you grip turns a greeting into a crowding move.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Wringing hands before being called in
poseGallery.annotation: Wringing feeds the nerves and dampens the palms. Let your hands rest, and keep any cold drink in your left hand.

poseGallery.doCaption: Declining with a hand on the heart
poseGallery.annotation: A refusal with no alternative feels like a rejection. A hand on the heart and a smile says yes to the person while saying no to the touch.

poseGallery.dontCaption: A full handshake on a hospital ward
poseGallery.annotation: Where infection matters, less contact is kinder. A fist bump keeps some warmth at a fraction of the contact.

poseGallery.doCaption: A matched grip at arm's length
poseGallery.dontCaption: Pulling someone in by the hand
poseGallery.annotation: A handshake that moves the other person is read as control. Meet midway and let them keep their balance.

poseGallery.doCaption: An early hand on the heart and a smile
poseGallery.dontCaption: Folding the arms to dodge an offered hand
poseGallery.annotation: Declining well is about timing. Show your alternative before the other person's hand is fully out.

caseStudy:
Arjun, thirty-four, manages a team at an engineering firm and has always shaken hands with everyone. During the pandemic he stopped, and when restrictions lifted he went straight back to it. For months he did not notice that some people met his hand a little late, or not at all.

Then, at the start of a supplier meeting, he reached out to a woman from the other company. She hesitated, then said, smiling, that she didn't shake hands, and put her hand on her heart. Arjun froze with his hand in the air, said sorry twice, and spent the first ten minutes of the meeting feeling clumsy. Later he realised he had made the moment far more awkward than she had.

He changed his approach. Now, as he walks up to someone, he lets his hand start to come forward slowly and watches. If their hand comes up, he shakes it: whole hand, a matched grip, a couple of seconds. If it does not, he turns the movement into a hand on his chest and a nod, and says it's good to meet them. He has stopped apologising when a hand is not taken.

He also noticed that one of his engineers, Tom, had a crushing grip that made visitors wince, and that Tom's palms were often damp before presentations. Arjun told him, privately and lightly, about both. Tom was embarrassed, but he eased his grip and started carrying his coffee in his left hand.

When Arjun's father went into hospital that winter, Arjun found himself bumping fists with the nurses instead of shaking hands. It felt odd at first. By the end of the week it felt like the most natural greeting there.
observe: Notice the half second before a greeting this week, and who moves first to offer a hand.
Notice how different people respond to an offered hand: matching it, hesitating or offering something else.
Notice your own grip when you shake hands. Is it complete, matched and brief, or does it lean towards crushing or limp?
Notice your hands in the minutes before a stressful meeting, and whether they are cold, damp or busy.

drills.name: Grip Calibration
steps: Ask a friend or partner to shake hands with you five times.
Vary your grip from very light to very firm, and ask them to say which felt best.
Try matching their grip rather than setting your own.
Check that your whole palm meets theirs, not just your fingers.
Practise a two- or three-second shake with a look at their face, then stop.
variations: Ask two different people, one with smaller hands and one with larger, to rate your grip, and notice whether your matched grip changes between them.
Practise the full greeting with a friend, grip, a look at the face and their name said back, and ask which part they noticed most.
Shake hands with your left hand a few times, as you might with someone who offers theirs, so that it does not feel strange when it happens.

drills.name: The Slow Offer
steps: For three greetings this week, let your hand start to come forward slowly as you approach.
Watch what the other person's hand does.
If it comes up, shake it. If it stays down, turn the movement into a nod or a hand on your heart.
Note how each greeting felt, and whether any were awkward.
variations: At your next group event, use the slow offer with every person you greet, senior and junior, and note whether anyone's response surprised you.
Try the slow offer with someone you already know well, and notice whether they meet your hand, wave or hug instead.
Watch a host at an event greet a line of people, and note how they handle the people who do not raise a hand.

drills.name: A Warm Decline
steps: Write one sentence you could use to decline a handshake warmly, such as I'm not shaking hands at the moment, but it's very good to meet you.
Choose a gesture to go with it: a hand on your heart, a small wave or a nod.
Practise both in a mirror until the gesture comes early, before the other person's hand is fully out.
Rehearse it once with a friend who offers a hand.
Keep the sentence ready for when you are unwell or the other person is vulnerable.
variations: Practise your decline with three different gestures, a wave, a hand on the heart and a nod, and choose the one that feels most like you.
Ask a friend to press you after you decline, with a cheerful "Oh, come on", and practise answering warmly without giving way.
Write a version of your decline for a formal setting and one for a casual one, and keep both ready.

drills.name: Pre-Meeting Hands
steps: Before your next interview or important meeting, notice your hands in the ten minutes beforehand.
If they are wringing or fidgeting, let them rest still and open.
Hold any cold drink in your left hand.
Wipe your right palm discreetly just before you stand.
variations: Try the routine before a social event as well as a work one, and notice whether your hands feel different when the stakes are lower.
Time how long before a meeting you start to fidget, and move your tissue-and-dry routine to just before that point.
Notice whether holding something, such as a notebook or a folder, in your left hand while you wait helps your hands stay still.

quiz.q: A colleague insists that a really firm handshake, as strong as you can make it, is what makes a good impression. What does the evidence suggest?
options: He is right; the hardest grips made the best impressions in every study of handshakes
A complete, matched grip with eye contact makes a good impression, while crushing does not
Grip makes no difference at all, because people form impressions only from faces and voices
A limp grip is best, because it shows people that you are gentle and that you mean no harm
quiz.explain: Chaplin's coders rated firmness as a combination of a complete grip, vigour, duration and eye contact. A crushing grip is a different thing, and it is usually read as competition rather than confidence.

quiz.q: What did Stewart and colleagues find in their 2008 study of mock job interviews?
options: Handshakes had no link with hiring recommendations once dress and appearance were controlled
Better handshakes went with better hiring recommendations, even with appearance and dress controlled
Only men's handshakes mattered, because interviewers ignored women's handshakes entirely
Interviewers rated weak handshakes more highly, because they read them as signs of humility
quiz.explain: Students with better handshakes received more favourable recommendations, and the handshake carried part of the link between extraversion and those judgments. It may be a sign of social ease rather than a cause of success.

quiz.q: In Mela and Whitworth's study of greetings and bacteria, which greeting transferred the fewest bacteria?
options: The handshake, as long as the grip was kept firm and short
The high five, because the palms met so very briefly
The fist bump, which involved the smallest area of contact
All three greetings transferred about the same amount of bacteria
quiz.explain: The handshake transferred the most and the fist bump the least, with the high five in between. Longer and stronger handshakes transferred more. The study used gloves, so it shows the relative difference rather than the risk of any one greeting.

quiz.q: You are about to greet a visitor and are not sure whether she shakes hands. What fits this chapter best?
options: Let your hand start forward slowly, then shake or switch to a nod and a smile
Keep your hands down and wait for her to make the first move, however long it takes
Push your hand out quickly and firmly, so that she cannot hesitate or say no
Ask her directly and at length about her views on shaking hands before you start
quiz.explain: A slow offer gives the other person time to respond. If her hand comes up, shake it; if it does not, turning the movement into a nod or a hand on your heart keeps the greeting warm.

quiz.q: A man from another company declines your offered hand and places his hand on his heart instead. What is the most likely meaning?
options: He is signalling dislike and does not want to work with you
He is greeting you warmly in a way that does not involve touch
He is testing whether you will insist on shaking his hand anyway
He has misunderstood and expected you to bow to him first
quiz.explain: A hand on the heart is a complete, warm greeting in many cultures. People decline handshakes for reasons of faith, health or comfort, and the gesture says they are glad to meet you without the touch.

quiz.q: Which conclusion does Dolcos and colleagues' 2012 study of handshakes support?
options: A handshake guarantees that any meeting will have a good outcome
Handshakes matter only when the people involved already know each other
Watching a handshake made no difference to how encounters were judged
Observers judged encounters that began with a handshake more positively
quiz.explain: People watching animated scenes rated encounters that began with a handshake more favourably, and a handshake softened the impact of cold behaviour. The participants were observers, so the study does not show what happens in real meetings.

quiz.q: What did Chaplin and colleagues find about how consistent people's handshakes were?
options: Handshakes changed completely depending on which coder each person was greeting
The same person tended to shake hands the same way on different occasions
Handshakes were consistent only among men, while women's varied a great deal
Only the strength of the grip was consistent, while every other feature varied
quiz.explain: The same person tended to shake hands in the same way on different occasions and with different coders. A firm handshake, in the full sense, went with more favourable first impressions.

quiz.q: An interviewer offers his hand and the candidate declines warmly, explaining that someone at home is vulnerable to infection. What fits this chapter best?
options: Accept it at once, offer a nod, and judge the candidate only on the interview
Note it as a sign of low confidence, since a handshake shows how a person copes
Insist gently on shaking, since a brief handshake carries very little real risk
Ask for details of the illness so that the panel can decide whether it is genuine
quiz.explain: People decline handshakes for health, faith and many other reasons, and since 2020 the handshake is one option among several. Accepting the decline and judging the answers is fair to the candidate.

quiz.q: Someone says that turning your hand palm down on top of the other person's is a proven way to show dominance. What does this chapter say?
options: That the move has been proven to make the other person defer to you in any negotiation that follows
That such claims are little tested, though grips that make people feel handled read as power plays
That palm-down handshakes are always read as warm and friendly by the person receiving them
That the direction of the palm makes no difference at all to how any handshake is ever read
quiz.explain: Ideas about palm-down grips and two-handed shakes are widely repeated but little tested. What is clearer is that a greeting which makes someone feel handled is read as a power play.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific greeting at work in the last month that felt awkward: a missed hand, a hesitation, a grip that was too hard or too limp. Describe who moved first, what each of you did with your hands and how the moment ended. What would a slow offer have changed? Then describe how you would decline a handshake warmly if you needed to, and what words and gesture you would use.
reflection.guidance: Awkward greetings are common and usually forgotten quickly, so there is nothing to be embarrassed about. The point is to notice your own habits: whether you reach too fast, grip too hard, or freeze when a hand is not met. Be specific about the moment, including where you were standing and what was said.

failureMode: The first failure is to treat firm as meaning hard, and to crush hands as a show of strength. The second is to push a hand out quickly and expect it to be taken, leaving the other person to refuse an offer they never wanted. The third is to take a declined handshake as an insult, when the reason is usually faith, health or comfort. The fourth is to make the moment worse with repeated apologies, when a smile and a warm word would let it pass. The fifth is to put a full handshake on someone who is ill, frail or in hospital, when a lighter greeting would be kinder. And the sixth is to believe a perfect grip will win an interview, when it is at most one small sign of being at ease.

moreCases.title: The candidate with damp palms
moreCases.scene:
Kwame, twenty-three, has a final-round interview for a graduate scheme at a large accountancy firm. He has prepared for weeks. He has also
  read, in three separate articles, that a weak or damp handshake can cost you a job in the first few seconds, and that interviewers judge your
  confidence by your grip. His palms sweat when he is nervous, and they have sweated at every interview he can remember.

  In the reception area, he sits with a cup of water from the cooler in his right hand, rubbing his left palm on his trousers. When the interviewer,
  Mrs Akhtar, a partner in her fifties, comes out to collect him, he stands too quickly, swaps the cup to his left hand, wipes his right palm hard on
  his thigh in full view, and then offers it. It is cold and damp from the cup. He apologises for it. She smiles, shakes it briefly and leads him to
  the lift.

  In the lift he cannot stop thinking about the handshake. He is sure it has already lost him the job. For the first ten minutes of the interview, he
  answers in short, careful sentences, waiting for the moment when she will mention it.

  She never does. Halfway through the interview, she asks him a question about a group project he led at university, and he forgets about his hands
  altogether for the first time that day.

His older sister, who works in recruitment, had told him on the phone the night before not to worry about his hands. He had thanked her and gone back to reading the articles.

He has also practised his grip on his flatmate, who told him it was fine and then, when pressed, that it was "a bit intense". Kwame has spent the week trying to find the exact point between intense and limp.
moreCases.misread:
Kwame read his damp handshake as a fatal first impression and spent the first part of the interview defending against a judgment that had not been made. He read the articles' warnings as rules that interviewers apply.

And he read Mrs Akhtar's smile as politeness covering a bad impression, when it was simply how she greeted every candidate.

The articles had taught him that a handshake was a test with a pass mark, when for most interviewers it is simply a way of saying hello. He read every second of the lift ride through that lesson, and arrived in the interview room already defeated by a judgment that existed only in his head.
moreCases.betterRead:
Stewart and colleagues did find that students with better handshakes got more favourable hiring recommendations in mock interviews, but the handshake seemed to carry part of a link with extraversion and ease, not to work as a test on its own. A brief damp handshake is one small sign among dozens, and most interviewers forget it long before they score anything. The bigger cost was the worry. Kwame's better routine, which he used at his next interview, was simple: hold any cold drink in his left hand, keep a tissue in his pocket and dry his palm discreetly a minute before he was called, stand at an ordinary pace, and say nothing about his hand. Mrs Akhtar's firm offered him a place. When he asked her, a year later, whether she had noticed the handshake, she said she remembered the group project answer.

He also stopped reading handshake articles the week before interviews, which he said was the best preparation of all.

moreCases.title: The hand that hurt
moreCases.scene:
Pauline, fifty-eight, is a partner at a firm of accountants, and she has had rheumatoid arthritis in her hands for nine years. On good days
  her knuckles ache; on bad days they are swollen and hot, and a firm squeeze makes her eyes water. Most of her work is with clients she knows, who
  have learned to greet her with a nod or a gentle touch. New clients are another matter.

  At a business breakfast, a new client, Steve, sixty, who runs a haulage company, strides up to her with his hand already out. Before she can
  say anything, he takes her hand and squeezes it hard, pumping it three times. The pain is sharp. She flinches, pulls her hand back and holds it
  against her chest, and for a second she cannot speak.

  Steve, who has always believed that a strong handshake shows respect, is taken aback. He reads her flinch and her pulled-back hand as a rebuff,
  and wonders whether she has taken against him, or against his company, or against men like him. He is stiff with her for the rest of the meeting.

  On the drive back to the office, Pauline's colleague asks her why she did not say anything. Pauline says that she never knows how to explain
  her hands to strangers without sounding as though she is making a fuss.

She has tried wearing a wrist support to signal her joints, but people do not seem to notice it until after they have squeezed.

Steve notices that Pauline barely looks at him during the meeting and keeps her right hand in her lap. He takes both as confirmation. In fact she is waiting for the pain to fade, and trying not to let it show.
moreCases.misread:
Steve read Pauline's flinch and withdrawn hand as a rejection, perhaps of him personally, and became cold with her for the rest of the meeting. He read his own crushing grip as the respectful greeting he had always been taught.

Pauline read her own silence as the only option, when a few words early would have spared her the squeeze.

Steve also read his own forty years of firm handshakes, and the fact that nobody had complained, as evidence that they were welcome. Silence about a painful grip is not the same as approval, and many people simply put up with it.
moreCases.betterRead:
Chaplin and colleagues' work suggests that a good handshake is complete, matched and brief, not hard. A grip strong enough to hurt says more about the person giving it than the person receiving it, and for people with arthritis, injuries or pain in their hands it can do real harm. The better reading was that Pauline's flinch was pain, not dislike. Her better approach, which a physiotherapist suggested, was to get in first: to lift her hand to her chest or offer a small wave as someone approached, and say warmly, "I don't shake hands, my joints won't let me, but it's lovely to meet you." Steve, when Pauline explained at their next meeting, was mortified. He told her that he had been squeezing hands hard for forty years and that nobody had ever told him it hurt. He has eased his grip since, and now waits to see what the other person does.

Pauline now gets in first at every new meeting, and finds that most people are relieved to be told.

moreCases.title: The chief executive's double grip
moreCases.scene:
Rob, forty-nine, has just become chief executive of a regional chain of garden centres. In his first month he visits all fourteen sites, and at
  each one he greets the staff individually. He has read that a two-handed shake shows warmth, so he takes each person's right hand in his, puts his
  left hand on their elbow or upper arm, and holds on while he asks their name and how long they have worked there. With the younger staff he sometimes
  adds a pat on the shoulder as he moves on.

  He believes the visits are going well. People smile and answer his questions, and the regional managers tell him that the staff appreciate his
  making the effort.

  The staff survey that follows tells a different story. Several comments mention the handshake. One says it felt "like being handled". Another says
  that he held on so long she did not know how to get her hand back. A third, from a man in his sixties who has worked at the same site for thirty
  years, says that being patted on the shoulder by a new boss half his age made him feel like a boy.

  Rob's head of people, Fatima, brings him the comments. He is surprised and a little defensive. He had meant every greeting kindly, and he had
  thought the extra hand was the kind part.

Rob learned the double grip from a sales trainer twenty years ago, who told him it was the handshake of a politician. He has never asked himself whether that was a recommendation.

Fatima also points out that several of the staff who wrote the comments are women, and that two of them had told her separately that they had not felt able to pull their hands away from the new boss.
moreCases.misread:
Rob read his two-handed grip and the pat on the shoulder as warmth, and read the staff's smiles during the visits as agreement. Many of the staff read the same gestures as control, and in the case of the oldest, as being talked down to.

The regional managers read the visits as a success because the staff were polite, which is what staff are with a new chief executive.

Rob read the defensive feeling he had when he saw the comments as a sign that the staff were being unfair, when it was the ordinary sting of learning that a kindness had not landed.
moreCases.betterRead:
Popular books describe the two-handed shake, the hand on the elbow and the pat as warm or as dominant, and the ideas are little tested. What is clear is that a handshake which makes the other person feel managed tends to be read as a power play, however it was meant, and that the more senior the person doing it, the more strongly it reads that way. Holding on too long removes the other person's choice about when the greeting ends. Fatima's better advice was to let warmth come from his face, his words and his attention: a single, matched, brief handshake if it was offered, a look at the person's face, their name repeated, and a real question. Rob tried it at the next round of visits. The comments the following year were about the questions he had asked, and one person wrote that he seemed to listen.

He also stopped patting people on the shoulder, which, he admitted, he had copied from a politician on television.

moreCases.title: The candidate who declined
moreCases.scene:
Dev, thirty, is applying for a job as a project manager at a housing charity. His partner is having treatment that leaves her immune system
  very weak, and on her consultant's advice the household is careful about infections. Dev has not shaken hands with anyone for over a year. He uses
  a small wave, a nod or a hand on his chest instead.

  The interviewer, Ian, sixty-one, is a director who has been interviewing people for thirty years and has a firm belief that you can tell a lot
  about a person from their handshake. When Dev comes into the room, Ian stands, walks round the desk and holds out his hand.

  Dev has prepared for this. He raises his hand in a small wave, smiles, and says, "I'm sorry, I'm not shaking hands at the moment, there's someone
  at home I need to be careful for. It's very good to meet you." Ian pauses for a second, says "Of course," and sits down.

  Afterwards, Ian tells the second panellist, Claire, that the candidate seemed a bit odd, and that he could not quite put his finger on why. He
  wonders whether Dev lacks confidence. Claire points out that Dev's answers were the strongest of the day, and that Ian himself had used the word
  "odd" about every candidate who had not shaken his hand that year.

Dev had thought about simply shaking hands for the interview and then washing them. He decided that his partner's safety was not something to bargain with for a first impression.

Ian has a habit, which he is proud of, of noting his first impression of every candidate within the first minute, before they have answered a question. He says it is usually right.

Dev, for his part, leaves the interview unsure how the greeting landed. He noticed the pause before Ian said "Of course", and he spends the train journey home wondering whether it cost him.
moreCases.misread:
Ian read Dev's declined handshake as oddness and perhaps a lack of confidence, because for thirty years the handshake had been his first test of a candidate. He did not notice that the reading had nothing to do with anything Dev had said or done in the interview.

Ian also read his own unease as insight, the kind of gut feeling his long experience had taught him to trust.

He also missed the possibility that a candidate who could decline so calmly, in a stressful moment, was showing exactly the steadiness the job required.
moreCases.betterRead:
The handshake is no longer the single expected greeting. Since 2020 it has become one option among several, and people decline it for health, faith, disability, pain or caution on behalf of someone else. Dev did exactly what the chapter suggests: he declined early, warmly, with an alternative gesture and a short reason he was happy to give, though he did not owe one. The misreading was Ian's. Claire's better approach, which the charity adopted, was to remove the handshake from the assessment altogether: interviewers would let the candidate lead the greeting, and the panel would score answers against criteria agreed in advance. Dev got the job. Ian, to his credit, told Claire a month later that he had been wrong, and that he had started letting candidates choose.

The change cost the charity nothing, and it meant that candidates who could not or would not shake hands were judged on the same footing as everyone else, which is what a fair interview is meant to do.

workedReading.title: Hosting a visiting delegation
workedReading.scene:
Martin, forty-four, runs the partnerships team at a university, and on Wednesday morning he is hosting a delegation of six visitors from a partner university abroad: two senior professors, a young research manager, an administrator, a PhD student and an older man who chairs their board. He has been told the names and roles but nothing about how each person prefers to greet. He knows that some may shake hands, some may bow, some may prefer not to touch at all, and that the senior visitors will be watching how he treats the junior ones. He has ten minutes in the entrance hall before the group arrives, and he spends them thinking about the greetings rather than rehearsing his welcome speech, because the greetings will come first and everyone will remember them.

He has hosted delegations before and made mistakes: a handshake offered to a woman who did not shake hands with men, a joke about bowing that fell flat. He wants this one to begin without any of that, so that the visitors' first minute is spent feeling welcome rather than managing him.

He also reminds himself that he is the host, which means the visitors should never have to wonder what is expected of them.

steps.label: Let the senior guest lead
steps.text:
The chair of the board comes through the door first. Martin walks towards him at an easy pace and lets his right hand begin to come forward slowly, low and open, without pushing it out. The older man stops, smiles and bows his head slightly. Martin turns his movement into a small bow of his own and says, "Welcome, it's an honour to have you here." Letting the most senior guest set the greeting is rarely wrong.

He also takes care with his pace. Striding up to the chair with his hand out would force a decision on an older man who has been travelling for a day. Walking at an easy pace gives the guest time to choose.

steps.label: Match the grip offered
steps.text:
One of the professors reaches out a hand straight away. Martin takes it with his whole palm, matches her grip rather than setting his own, looks at her face and says her name. Two or three seconds, then he lets go. Chaplin and colleagues found that a firm handshake in the full sense, complete, matched and brief with eye contact, went with better first impressions. Martin keeps it ordinary.

He resists the urge to add a second hand or a squeeze for emphasis. With a senior visitor watching, a simple, matched greeting says more about his respect than any flourish.

steps.label: Read the hand that stays down
steps.text:
The administrator, a woman in her forties, keeps her hands together in front of her and places one lightly on her chest as Martin turns to her. He sees it early, does not offer his hand, places his own on his chest and nods. "Lovely to meet you." He does not apologise or comment. She smiles. Whatever her reason, faith, health or preference, it is hers, and he does not need to know it.

He also notes, for later, that she may prefer not to be seated where she will be crowded or touched in passing, and quietly makes sure she has space at the lunch table.

steps.label: Greet everyone the same way
steps.text:
The PhD student is at the back, half-hidden behind the others. Martin goes to him as deliberately as he went to the chair, waits to see what he offers and receives a fist bump, which he returns. He knows that in a group, people notice whom you greet fully and whom you skip, and that a host who greets the senior visitors warmly and nods at the juniors is telling everyone how he ranks them.

He also introduces the student to a colleague by name, so that the young man is drawn into the group rather than left at its edge. A greeting is the start of including someone, not the whole of it.

steps.label: Recover from a collision
steps.text:
The research manager and Martin both reach at the same moment, he for a handshake and she for a nod, and his hand ends up in the air. He laughs lightly, turns it into a small wave and says, "We'll call that one a wave." She laughs too. A single light word and a smile let the moment pass; repeated apologies would have made it bigger than it was.

He notices that the research manager seems slightly embarrassed, and makes a point of asking her a question about her work a few minutes later, so that the collision is not the last thing she remembers about meeting him.

steps.label: Plan the goodbye
steps.text:
At the end of the day, the group gathers in the entrance hall again. Martin remembers how each person greeted him that morning and follows the same pattern for the farewells: a bow for the chair, a handshake for the professor, a hand on the heart for the administrator, a fist bump for the student. Greetings at the end of a visit are often warmer than at the start, and he lets his face show that he enjoyed the day.

He also says each person's name as he says goodbye, which tells them that the morning's greeting was not a formality and that he remembered who they were.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
The chair of the board writes afterwards to thank the university, and mentions the warmth of the welcome. The administrator tells Martin's colleague over coffee that many hosts had tried to shake her hand and that she had been grateful not to have to refuse. Martin writes himself a note for next time: start slowly, let them lead, greet the back of the group as carefully as the front, laugh off the collisions, and remember who did what for the goodbye.

He realises that he spent almost no time thinking about grip, and almost all of it watching people's hands and faces in the second before they met. That second, he decides, is where the greeting happens now.

moreFailures.title: Shaking some hands and not others
moreFailures.body:
In a group, people notice the pattern of your greetings as much as each greeting. A man who shakes hands with every man in the room and nods at the women, who greets the senior visitors fully and waves at the juniors, or who shakes hands with everyone except the colleague in the wheelchair, is sending a message about whom he counts, whatever he intends. Sometimes the pattern comes from a reasonable worry about getting it wrong, for example about whether a woman in a headscarf shakes hands. The answer is not to skip her but to approach everyone in the same way: walk up, let your hand begin to come forward slowly and let each person lead. That way every greeting starts with the same offer, and each person's answer is respected. Watch yourself at the next group event and notice who gets what.

If you are not sure, it is better to offer the same slow, open beginning to everyone and be declined than to decide on someone's behalf that they would not want it.

moreFailures.title: Using the handshake to manage people
moreFailures.body:
The handshake can be used to make a point: a grip that turns the other person's hand palm up, a second hand clamped on their wrist or elbow, a pull that brings them off balance towards you, a shake that goes on until you decide it ends, a pat on the shoulder as you move on. Popular books describe some of these as dominance moves, and while the specific claims are little tested, the general effect is clear enough: a greeting that makes the other person feel handled tends to be read as a power play. It also tends to be remembered. If you are senior, the effect is stronger, because the other person cannot easily resist. Let the handshake be a simple, matched, brief greeting, and let warmth come from your face, your words and your attention, as Rob learned at the garden centres.

If you notice yourself reaching for the other person's arm or shoulder, ask whether you would like the same from someone you had just met.

A handshake should leave the other person exactly where they were standing, with their hand back and their dignity intact.

moreFailures.title: Watching the hands and forgetting the face
moreFailures.body:
Many people concentrate so hard on getting the grip right that they forget the rest of the greeting. They look at the hands, or past the person to the next one, and say nothing, or mumble their name. But a greeting is more than a grip. Chaplin and colleagues' definition of a firm handshake included eye contact, and much of what makes a first meeting feel warm is in the face and the voice: a look at the person, a smile that reaches the eyes, their name said back to them, a short sentence that shows you are glad to meet them. If you have to choose where to put your attention in the half second of a greeting, put it on the person's face, not their hand. A slightly imperfect grip with a warm look is far better than a perfect grip with a vacant one.

It also helps to say your own name clearly as you greet, so that the other person does not have to ask or pretend they caught it.

moreFailures.title: Pressing after a decline
moreFailures.body:
When someone declines a handshake, some people push back: "Oh, come on, I don't bite," "I've had my jab," "Just this once." It is usually meant as friendly teasing. It is not received that way. It puts the other person in the position of refusing twice, often in front of others, and it treats their decision as something to be argued with. For someone who declines for reasons of faith, it can feel like disrespect for their beliefs; for someone with pain, a health risk or a history that makes touch unwelcome, it can feel like pressure on a boundary. The kind response to a decline is the same whatever the reason: accept it at once, offer an alternative, such as a nod or a hand on your heart, say something warm and move on. You do not need to know why, and you do not need to win.

If you are the one declining and someone presses, it is fine to repeat yourself once, kindly and firmly, and then change the subject.

questions.q: How long should a handshake last?
questions.a:
A couple of seconds, usually with no more than two or three small movements up and down. Chaplin and colleagues included a reasonable duration in their definition of a good handshake, and the commonest complaints about bad handshakes include the pump that goes on too long and the grip that will not let go. The simplest rule is to match the other person: shake while they shake and release when they begin to release. If you are holding someone's hand while you finish a sentence, you are probably holding it too long. Let go, keep looking at them and finish the sentence with your hands at your sides. The warmth of a greeting comes from the face and the words, not from the length of the grip.

In some places and settings, greetings last longer, with a lingering hand or a hand held while talking. Follow the other person's lead and let them decide when it ends.

questions.q: What can I do about sweaty hands?
questions.a:
Quite a lot, and most of it is simple. Hold any cold drink in your left hand, so that your right one stays dry and warm. Keep a tissue or a handkerchief in your pocket, and dry your palm discreetly a minute or two before you stand, rather than wiping it on your trousers in front of the other person. Keep your hands still and open while you wait, rather than clasped or wringing, which tends to make them warmer and damper. Above all, do not apologise for your hand: most people barely notice a slightly damp palm, and an apology draws attention to it. If sweating is severe and troubles you a great deal, it is worth talking to your doctor, because there are treatments that can help.

It also helps to know that many people's palms are damp when they are nervous, including interviewers, so you are far from alone.

questions.q: Should I still expect to shake hands at a job interview?
questions.a:
Be ready to, but let the interviewer lead. Many interviewers still offer a hand, and Stewart and colleagues' work suggests that an easy, complete handshake can be part of an impression of being at ease. But many now do not, and a growing number of organisations have removed the handshake from interviews altogether. Walk in at an ordinary pace, let your hand begin to come forward slowly, and follow what the interviewer does. If you do not shake hands yourself, for health, faith or any other reason, decline early and warmly with an alternative, as Dev did, and do not apologise more than once. Any interviewer who marks you down for it is judging something that has nothing to do with the job.

And remember that your answers will be scored for far longer than your handshake will be remembered.

questions.q: How should I greet someone whose hands or arms are affected by a disability?
questions.a:
Much as you would greet anyone else, but with extra attention to their lead. Offer your hand slowly, if it seems natural, and let them decide. Someone with limited use of their right hand may offer their left, which is perfectly fine to shake; someone with a prosthetic arm may offer it or may prefer a nod; someone who cannot shake may smile or say hello, and that is the greeting. Do not grab, steer or help unless asked. If someone cannot see, say your name as you approach and say that you are offering your hand, so that they can find it or decline. The aim is the same as with every greeting in this chapter: give the other person the choice, and follow it without fuss.

It also helps to keep your own hands visible and still as you approach, so that the other person can see what you are offering.

questions.q: Is a fist bump too casual for work?
questions.a:
It depends on the setting. In hospitals and care homes, where staff greet many people and infection matters, the fist bump is a sensible choice, and Mela and Whitworth's study found that it transferred far fewer bacteria than a handshake. It is also common in sport, in many younger workplaces and among friends. In a formal meeting with people you do not know, it may read as too casual, and a handshake, a nod or a hand on the heart may fit better. The safest approach is the same as always: let the other person lead. If they offer a fist, bump it; if they offer a hand, shake it; if you are not sure, start slowly and see.

In mixed settings, such as a hospital meeting with outside visitors, it is fine to offer the fist bump and explain why.

Whatever you choose, do it with the same warmth you would bring to a handshake: a look at the face, a smile and a word.

questions.q: Is it rude to decline a handshake?
questions.a:
No, as long as you do it warmly. People decline for many good reasons: faith, health, pain, disability, protecting someone vulnerable, or simply preferring not to touch strangers. What makes a decline feel rude is not the decision but the delivery: a hand left hanging, a step back, a frown, or silence. Decline early, before the other person's hand is fully out, by raising your own hand in a small wave or placing it on your chest, and pair it with a warm sentence, such as "I don't shake hands, but it's lovely to meet you." You can give a reason if you want to, but you do not owe one. Most people accept it immediately, and the ones who do not are showing you something about themselves.

And if you host events, it helps to make declining easy for everyone, for example by greeting with a nod and a smile yourself.

If you are the one offering and it is declined, the same applies in reverse: accept it at once and say something warm.

watch.title: Trump and Macron share long handshake
watch.notice: A handshake between two presidents that becomes a contest of grip and duration. Notice the knuckles, the pull, and who lets go first.

reviewPrompt: This week, offer your hand slowly and watch for the other person's answer, and have one warm way of declining ready.
